content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums of length n, return an array of length 2n where ans[i] = nums[i] and ans[i+n] = nums[i] for 0 <= i < n.
content.naiveApproach: Allocate a new array of size 2n, copy nums twice into it.
content.optimizedApproach: Same single-pass copy — there is no complexity improvement possible beyond O(n).
content.keyInsight: The answer is simply nums + nums. In Python: return nums + nums.
content.pseudocode: return nums + nums
followUpQuestions: What if you needed k repetitions?
Can you do it in-place if the array has extra space?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.
content.naiveApproach: Sort the array then compare adjacent elements — O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.
content.optimizedApproach: Use a hash set. For each number, check if it's already in the set; if yes return true, else add it.
content.keyInsight: A set gives O(1) lookup. Return true as soon as a duplicate is found — no need to finish the scan.
content.pseudocode:
seen = set()
for n in nums:
    if n in seen: return True
    seen.add(n)
return False
followUpQuestions: Contains Duplicate II — what if duplicates must be within k indices?
What if nums is a stream?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if there are two distinct indices i and j such that nums[i] == nums[j] and abs(i - j) <= k.
content.naiveApproach: For every pair (i, j) check if values equal and distance ≤ k. O(n·k) time.
content.optimizedApproach: Use a sliding window hash map of size k: store value → index. If nums[i] exists in the map and i - map[v] <= k, return true; otherwise update map[v] = i.
content.keyInsight: Maintain only the most recent index for each value. The window constraint means you only need to keep k entries.
followUpQuestions: Extend to |nums[i] - nums[j]| <= t and |i - j| <= k (Contains Duplicate III)?

content.problemStatement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses the same characters in any order.
content.constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 5 * 10^4
s and t consist of lowercase English letters
content.naiveApproach: Sort both strings and compare. O(n log n).
content.optimizedApproach: Count character frequencies using a hash map (or a 26-element array). Compare counts.
content.keyInsight: Two strings are anagrams iff they have identical character frequency maps. An array of 26 ints is enough for lowercase letters.
content.pseudocode:
if len(s) != len(t): return False
count = [0]*26
for c in s: count[ord(c)-ord('a')] += 1
for c in t: count[ord(c)-ord('a')] -= 1
return all(x == 0 for x in count)
followUpQuestions: How would you handle Unicode characters?

content.problemStatement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution; you may not use the same element twice.
content.naiveApproach: Check every pair (i, j) with i < j and see if nums[i] + nums[j] == target. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Build a hash map value → index as you iterate. For each num, check if (target - num) is already in the map.
content.keyInsight: Build the complement map on-the-fly — check before inserting to avoid using the same element twice.
followUpQuestions: What if the array is sorted? (Two Sum II)

content.problemStatement: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order.
content.constraints:
1 <= strs.length <= 10^4
0 <= strs[i].length <= 100
strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters
content.naiveApproach: For each pair of strings check if they are anagrams by sorting both. O(n² · k log k).
content.optimizedApproach: Use a hash map keyed by either (a) sorted string or (b) tuple of 26-char counts. All strings with the same key are anagrams.
content.keyInsight: Sorting each string gives a canonical form. Alternatively, a 26-element frequency tuple avoids sorting and runs O(n·k).
followUpQuestions: How do you handle non-ASCII characters?
What if you want groups sorted alphabetically?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
content.constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
k is in range [1, number of unique elements]
Answer is guaranteed to be unique
content.naiveApproach: Count frequencies with a map, sort by frequency descending, return first k. O(n log n).
content.optimizedApproach: Bucket sort by frequency: create n+1 buckets indexed by count, place each element in its bucket, then scan right-to-left collecting k elements.
content.keyInsight: Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucket sort achieves O(n). A min-heap of size k gives O(n log k) which is also better than full sort.
followUpQuestions: What if k is close to n (use sort)?
Top k frequent words — same approach with lexicographic tiebreak?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. Solve in O(n) without division.
content.constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-30 <= nums[i] <= 30
Guaranteed product fits in a 32-bit integer
content.naiveApproach: For each index, multiply all other elements. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Two-pass prefix/suffix product. Forward pass builds prefix products; backward pass multiplies suffix products into the result array.
content.keyInsight: answer[i] = (product of all elements left of i) * (product of all elements right of i). The output array itself serves as the prefix product store.
content.pseudocode:
n = len(nums)
res = [1]*n
prefix = 1
for i in range(n):
    res[i] = prefix
    prefix *= nums[i]
suffix = 1
for i in range(n-1,-1,-1):
    res[i] *= suffix
    suffix *= nums[i]
return res
followUpQuestions: What if zeros appear in nums?
Can you handle with division if no zeros?

content.problemStatement: Determine if a 9×9 Sudoku board is valid. Each row, column, and 3×3 sub-box must contain digits 1-9 without repetition. Empty cells are represented by '.'.
content.constraints:
board.length == 9, board[i].length == 9
board[i][j] is a digit or '.'
content.naiveApproach: Three nested loops — one for rows, one for cols, one for boxes. Each loop checks a separate set. Still O(1) for a fixed 9×9 board.
content.optimizedApproach: Single pass: maintain three 9×9 boolean grids (rows, cols, boxes). For cell (r,c) the box index is (r//3)*3 + c//3.
content.keyInsight: Box index = (row // 3) * 3 + (col // 3). Everything is fixed-size (9), so it's technically O(1) but the formula is the key insight.
content.pseudocode:
rows = defaultdict(set)
cols = defaultdict(set)
boxes = defaultdict(set)
for r in range(9):
    for c in range(9):
        v = board[r][c]
        if v == '.': continue
        box = (r//3, c//3)
        if v in rows[r] or v in cols[c] or v in boxes[box]:
            return False
        rows[r].add(v); cols[c].add(v); boxes[box].add(v)
return True
followUpQuestions: How would you solve a Sudoku (Sudoku Solver 37)?
How do you validate a partially filled board?

content.problemStatement: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings to a single string. The encoded string is then transmitted and decoded back to the original list of strings.
content.constraints:
1 <= strs.length <= 200
0 <= strs[i].length <= 200
strs[i] contains any possible characters including special characters
content.naiveApproach: Join with a delimiter (e.g. '#') — but fails if strings contain '#'.
content.optimizedApproach: Length-prefix encoding: for each string, prepend its length and a delimiter (e.g. '4#neet'). Decoder reads length, skips '#', reads that many chars.
content.keyInsight: Any delimiter can appear in the string itself. Use a length prefix so the decoder knows exactly how many bytes to read — delimiter ambiguity disappears.
content.pseudocode:
# Encode
res = ''
for s in strs:
    res += str(len(s)) + '#' + s
return res
# Decode
strs, i = [], 0
while i < len(s):
    j = s.index('#', i)
    length = int(s[i:j])
    strs.append(s[j+1:j+1+length])
    i = j + 1 + length
return strs
followUpQuestions: How would you handle binary data (not just strings)?
What if you needed random access to the i-th string without full decode?

content.problemStatement: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. Must run in O(n) time.
content.naiveApproach: Sort and scan for the longest run. O(n log n).
content.optimizedApproach: Put all numbers in a hash set. For each number n, if n-1 is NOT in the set then n is a sequence start — count forward until the sequence breaks.
content.keyInsight: Only start counting from the beginning of a sequence (when n-1 is absent). This ensures each element is visited at most twice total.
followUpQuestions: Can you recover the actual sequence, not just its length?
What if duplicates affect the answer?

content.problemStatement: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element — the element that appears more than ⌊n/2⌋ times. The majority element always exists.
content.naiveApproach: Count each element with a hash map and return the one with count > n/2. O(n) time, O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Boyer-Moore Voting: maintain a candidate and count. When count reaches 0, pick current element as candidate. The survivor is the majority element.
content.keyInsight: Since majority appears > n/2 times, it can 'survive' pairing off against all other elements. Boyer-Moore exploits this guarantee.
followUpQuestions: What if no guaranteed majority (verify after)? (Majority Element II)
Extend to elements appearing > n/3 times?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array of size n, find all elements that appear more than ⌊n/3⌋ times.
content.naiveApproach: Hash map counting, then filter by count > n/3. O(n) time, O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Extended Boyer-Moore with two candidate/count pairs. At most 2 elements can appear more than n/3 times.
content.keyInsight: There can be at most ⌊3/1⌋ - 1 = 2 majority candidates. Track two candidates simultaneously, then verify their actual counts.
content.pseudocode:
c1, c2, cnt1, cnt2 = None, None, 0, 0
for n in nums:
    if n==c1: cnt1+=1
    elif n==c2: cnt2+=1
    elif cnt1==0: c1,cnt1=n,1
    elif cnt2==0: c2,cnt2=n,1
    else: cnt1-=1; cnt2-=1
return [c for c in (c1,c2) if nums.count(c)>len(nums)//3]
followUpQuestions: What about elements appearing > n/k times (generalize)?

content.problemStatement: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array.
content.constraints:
n == nums.length
1 <= n <= 10^4
0 <= nums[i] <= n
All numbers are distinct
content.naiveApproach: Sort and scan for the gap. O(n log n).
content.optimizedApproach: Expected sum of [0..n] is n*(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum to get the missing number.
content.keyInsight: Gauss formula: sum(0..n) = n*(n+1)//2. The difference is the missing element. XOR approach also works: XOR all indices and all values.
content.pseudocode: return n*(n+1)//2 - sum(nums)
followUpQuestions: What if two numbers are missing? (Find All Numbers Disappeared)
How to do it with XOR?

content.problemStatement: You are given a large integer represented as an integer array digits, where each digits[i] is the i-th digit. Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array.
content.constraints:
1 <= digits.length <= 100
0 <= digits[i] <= 9
digits does not contain leading zeros
content.naiveApproach: Convert array to integer, add 1, convert back. Fails for very large numbers beyond int range.
content.optimizedApproach: Walk from the rightmost digit. If digit < 9, increment and return. If digit == 9, set to 0 and carry to next digit. If carry propagates past index 0, prepend 1.
content.keyInsight: Only carry propagates; in the worst case (all 9s), the array grows by one digit.
followUpQuestions: Add Two Numbers represented as linked lists (2)?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, rotate the array to the right by k steps, where k is non-negative.
content.naiveApproach: Rotate one step at a time, k times. O(n*k).
content.optimizedApproach: Three reverses: (1) reverse entire array, (2) reverse first k elements, (3) reverse remaining n-k elements. k = k % n first.
content.keyInsight: The three-reverse trick works because rotating right by k is equivalent to: reverse all, reverse [0..k-1], reverse [k..n-1].
content.pseudocode:
k %= len(nums)
nums.reverse()
nums[:k] = nums[:k][::-1]
nums[k:] = nums[k:][::-1]
followUpQuestions: What if you can't modify the array in-place?

content.problemStatement: A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome.
content.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 2 * 10^5
s consists only of printable ASCII characters
content.naiveApproach: Clean the string (filter + lower), then check s == s[::-1]. O(n) but creates a copy.
content.optimizedApproach: Two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters. Compare characters in-place.
content.keyInsight: Two pointers avoid allocating a cleaned copy. Skip non-alphanumeric with a helper and compare case-insensitively.
content.pseudocode:
l, r = 0, len(s)-1
while l < r:
    while l<r and not s[l].isalnum(): l+=1
    while l<r and not s[r].isalnum(): r-=1
    if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower(): return False
    l+=1; r-=1
return True
followUpQuestions: Valid Palindrome II — can remove at most one character?

content.problemStatement: Given a string s, return true if the s can be palindrome after deleting at most one character from it.
content.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
s consists of lowercase English letters
content.naiveApproach: Try removing each character and check if result is a palindrome. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Two pointers. On mismatch, try skipping left char OR skipping right char — check if either resulting substring is a palindrome. O(n).
content.keyInsight: On the first mismatch you have only two choices: skip left or skip right. Check both and return true if either is a palindrome.
followUpQuestions: Extend to at most k deletions?

content.problemTitle: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
content.problemStatement: Given a 1-indexed sorted array of integers numbers, find two numbers that add up to target. Return their indices as [index1, index2]. Use only constant extra space.
content.constraints:
2 <= numbers.length <= 3 * 10^4
-1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000
-1000 <= target <= 1000
Exactly one solution exists
content.naiveApproach: Hash map (same as Two Sum). Works but uses O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Two pointers from both ends. If sum < target, move left pointer right; if sum > target, move right pointer left.
content.keyInsight: Sorted order lets two pointers converge: a larger left sum means move left forward, a smaller means move right backward.
content.pseudocode:
l, r = 0, len(numbers)-1
while l < r:
    s = numbers[l] + numbers[r]
    if s == target: return [l+1, r+1]
    elif s < target: l+=1
    else: r-=1
followUpQuestions: Two Sum on unsorted array (hash map)?

content.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. Return no duplicate triplets.
content.naiveApproach: Three nested loops checking all triplets, then deduplicate with a set. O(n³).
content.optimizedApproach: Sort the array. For each index i, run two-pointer on the rest. Skip duplicates at each level.
content.keyInsight: Fix the first element and reduce to a Two Sum II problem. Sort enables two pointers; duplicate skipping ensures unique triplets.
content.pseudocode:
nums.sort()
res = []
for i, v in enumerate(nums):
    if i > 0 and v == nums[i-1]: continue
    l, r = i+1, len(nums)-1
    while l < r:
        s = v + nums[l] + nums[r]
        if s < 0: l+=1
        elif s > 0: r-=1
        else:
            res.append([v,nums[l],nums[r]])
            l+=1
            while l<r and nums[l]==nums[l-1]: l+=1
return res

content.problemStatement: Given an array nums of n integers and target, return all unique quadruplets [a,b,c,d] such that a+b+c+d == target.
content.naiveApproach: Four nested loops, deduplicate with a set. O(n⁴).
content.optimizedApproach: Sort, fix two outer loops with duplicate skipping, then use two-pointer for the inner pair. O(n³).
content.keyInsight: Generalize 3Sum: fix i and j, apply two-pointer on [j+1..n-1]. Avoid overflow by using long arithmetic for large values.
content.pseudocode:
nums.sort(); res = []
for i in range(len(nums)):
    if i>0 and nums[i]==nums[i-1]: continue
    for j in range(i+1,len(nums)):
        if j>i+1 and nums[j]==nums[j-1]: continue
        l, r = j+1, len(nums)-1
        while l<r:
            s=nums[i]+nums[j]+nums[l]+nums[r]
            if s<target: l+=1
            elif s>target: r-=1
            else:
                res.append([nums[i],nums[j],nums[l],nums[r]])
                l+=1
                while l<r and nums[l]==nums[l-1]: l+=1
return res

content.problemStatement: Given n non-negative integers representing heights, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water.
content.optimizedApproach: Two pointers at both ends. Move the pointer with the shorter height inward — any other move can only decrease width without guaranteed height gain.
content.keyInsight: Water = min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l). Moving the taller side can never improve: shrinking width while keeping the same min height only reduces area.
content.pseudocode:
l, r = 0, len(height)-1
res = 0
while l < r:
    res = max(res, min(height[l],height[r]) * (r-l))
    if height[l] <= height[r]: l+=1
    else: r-=1
return res
followUpQuestions: Can the greedy choice miss the optimum? (Proof by exchange argument)

content.problemStatement: Given an array nums with n objects colored red (0), white (1), or blue (2), sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent with order red, white, blue.
content.constraints:
n == nums.length
1 <= n <= 300
nums[i] is 0, 1, or 2
content.optimizedApproach: Dutch National Flag (Dijkstra). Three pointers: lo, mid, hi. Move 0s to lo, 2s to hi, 1s stay in middle. Single pass.
content.keyInsight: DNF algorithm: swap nums[mid] with nums[lo] for 0, swap with nums[hi] for 2, advance mid for 1. mid only advances when not a 2.
followUpQuestions: What if the three values are not 0,1,2 but arbitrary?

content.problemStatement: People[i] is the weight of the i-th person, and each boat can carry at most two people with weight limit. Return the minimum number of boats to carry every given person.
content.optimizedApproach: Sort people. Use two pointers: pair lightest with heaviest if their combined weight ≤ limit; otherwise send heaviest alone.
content.keyInsight: The greedy insight: always try to pair the heaviest person with the lightest. If they fit, great; if not, the heaviest goes alone.
content.pseudocode:
people.sort()
l, r = 0, len(people)-1
boats = 0
while l <= r:
    if people[l] + people[r] <= limit:
        l+=1
    r-=1
    boats+=1
return boats
followUpQuestions: What if boats can carry more than 2 people?

content.problemStatement: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
content.naiveApproach: For each bar, find max left and max right height, water = min(maxL,maxR) - height[i]. Use prefix/suffix arrays. O(n) time, O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Two pointers with running max left and max right. Process the side with smaller max first — the min is determined.
content.keyInsight: Water at position i is bounded by min(maxLeft, maxRight). Process whichever side has the smaller current max — its bound is guaranteed since the other side is at least as tall.
content.pseudocode:
l, r = 0, len(height)-1
maxL = maxR = res = 0
while l < r:
    if maxL <= maxR:
        if height[l] >= maxL: maxL = height[l]
        else: res += maxL - height[l]
        l+=1
    else:
        if height[r] >= maxR: maxR = height[r]
        else: res += maxR - height[r]
        r-=1
return res

content.problemTitle: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
content.problemStatement: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. Maximize profit by choosing a single day to buy and a later day to sell. Return 0 if no profit is possible.
content.optimizedApproach: Track the minimum price seen so far. For each day compute profit = price - minSoFar and update the answer.
content.keyInsight: We want max(prices[j] - prices[i]) for j > i. Greedy: keep the lowest price seen; the best sell is at the highest price after that point.
content.pseudocode:
min_price = float('inf')
max_profit = 0
for p in prices:
    min_price = min(min_price, p)
    max_profit = max(max_profit, p - min_price)
return max_profit

content.problemStatement: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
content.constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4
s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
content.naiveApproach: Check all substrings for uniqueness with a set. O(n²) or O(n³).
content.optimizedApproach: Sliding window with a hash map tracking the last seen index of each character. Move left pointer past the duplicate when one is found.
content.keyInsight: When a duplicate is found at position r, the left boundary jumps to max(left, last_seen[char]+1) — never moves backwards.
followUpQuestions: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters?

content.problemStatement: Given a string s and integer k, you can replace at most k characters in any window to make all characters the same. Return the length of the longest such window.
content.constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
s consists of uppercase English letters
0 <= k <= s.length
content.naiveApproach: Try all substrings and check if replaceable. O(n² * 26).
content.optimizedApproach: Sliding window with a frequency map. A window is valid if (window_size - max_freq) <= k. Expand right; if invalid, slide left.
content.keyInsight: The window size - count of the most frequent character = replacements needed. We never shrink the window below the current best size (only slide).
followUpQuestions: Longest subarray of 1s after deleting one element?
Minimum number of replacements to make string uniform?

content.problemStatement: Given two strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1 (i.e., one of s1's permutations is a substring of s2).
content.constraints:
1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 10^4
s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters
content.naiveApproach: Generate all permutations of s1 and check if any is a substring of s2. O(n! * m).
content.optimizedApproach: Fixed-size sliding window of length len(s1) over s2. Compare character frequency arrays.
content.keyInsight: Two strings are permutations of each other iff their character frequencies match. Maintain a running count with 'need' tracking how many chars still need matching.
content.pseudocode:
from collections import Counter
need = Counter(s1)
have = {}
formed = 0; k = len(s1)
for r in range(len(s2)):
    c = s2[r]
    have[c] = have.get(c,0)+1
    if c in need and have[c]==need[c]: formed+=1
    if r>=k:
        left=s2[r-k]
        if left in need and have[left]==need[left]: formed-=1
        have[left]-=1
    if formed==len(need): return True
return False

content.problemStatement: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. Return 0 if no such subarray exists.
content.naiveApproach: Check all subarrays with prefix sums. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Sliding window: expand right, shrink left while sum >= target keeping track of minimum length.
content.keyInsight: Since all values are positive, the window sum monotonically increases with expansion. Shrink from left to find the minimum valid window.
content.pseudocode:
l = total = 0
res = float('inf')
for r in range(len(nums)):
    total += nums[r]
    while total >= target:
        res = min(res, r-l+1)
        total -= nums[l]
        l+=1
return 0 if res==float('inf') else res
followUpQuestions: What if numbers can be negative? (Deque/monotonic approach)
Binary search on prefix sums O(n log n)?

content.problemStatement: Return the length of a maximum size turbulent subarray of arr. A subarray is turbulent if comparisons between consecutive elements strictly alternate between > and <.
content.naiveApproach: Check all subarrays for the turbulence property. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Sliding window: extend while the alternating property holds; reset when it breaks.
content.keyInsight: Compare the sign of arr[i-1]-arr[i] vs arr[i]-arr[i+1]. Reset the window start whenever the alternating pattern breaks or two consecutive elements are equal.
content.pseudocode:
l = res = 1
for r in range(1, len(arr)):
    if r==1 or arr[r-2]==arr[r-1] or \
       (arr[r-1]>arr[r-2])==(arr[r]>arr[r-1]):
        l = r
    res = max(res, r-l+1)
return res

content.problemStatement: Given strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t is included. If no such window exists, return empty string.
content.constraints:
m == s.length, n == t.length
1 <= m, n <= 10^5
s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters
content.naiveApproach: Check all substrings, verify each with Counter comparison. O(m² * n).
content.optimizedApproach: Sliding window with two counters: need (target freq) and have (window freq). Track 'formed' — count of chars meeting their target frequency. Shrink when all formed.
content.keyInsight: Track how many distinct characters have met their required frequency ('formed == len(need)'). When formed == required, try shrinking the left pointer.
content.pseudocode:
need=Counter(t); have={}; formed=l=0
resLen=float('inf'); resL=resR=0
for r,c in enumerate(s):
    have[c]=have.get(c,0)+1
    if c in need and have[c]==need[c]: formed+=1
    while formed==len(need):
        if r-l+1<resLen: resLen=r-l+1;resL=l;resR=r
        have[s[l]]-=1
        if s[l] in need and have[s[l]]<need[s[l]]: formed-=1
        l+=1
return '' if resLen==float('inf') else s[resL:resR+1]

content.problemStatement: You are given an array nums and an integer k. There is a sliding window of size k moving right, one step at a time. Return an array of the maximum values in each window.

content.problemStatement: Given a string s containing just '(', ')', '{', '}', '[', ']', determine if the input string is valid. Open brackets must be closed by the same type and in the correct order.

content.problemStatement: You are keeping score for a baseball game. Given a list of operations: integer (add score), '+' (sum of last two), 'D' (double last), 'C' (invalidate last). Return the sum of all scores.

content.keyInsight: A stack naturally models the 'last valid score' semantics needed for all four operations.

content.problemStatement: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin operations in O(1) time.

content.problemStatement: Given an array asteroids of integers representing asteroids in a row. Positive moves right, negative moves left. Equal-size asteroids explode each other. Return the state of asteroids after all collisions.
content.naiveApproach: Simulate with repeated passes until no more collisions. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Stack simulation. Collision only when stack top is positive and current is negative. Handle: right destroys left, left destroys right, or both destroy.
content.keyInsight: Only right-moving asteroid at top of stack vs left-moving current asteroid can collide. Three outcomes: current destroyed, top destroyed, or mutual destruction.

content.problemStatement: Given an array of temperatures, return an array answer where answer[i] is the number of days until a warmer temperature. If there is no future warmer day, answer[i] = 0.
content.naiveApproach: For each day, scan forward to find the next warmer day. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Monotonic stack (decreasing): push indices. When current temp > stack top's temp, pop and record the difference as the answer.
content.keyInsight: Stack tracks indices waiting for a warmer day. A warmer day 'resolves' all cooler days still in the stack.
content.pseudocode:
stack = []
res = [0]*len(temperatures)
for i, t in enumerate(temperatures):
    while stack and temperatures[stack[-1]] < t:
        j = stack.pop()
        res[j] = i - j
    stack.append(i)
return res

content.problemStatement: Given a string s containing '(', ')', and '*', return true if s is valid. '*' can be treated as '(', ')', or empty string.
content.naiveApproach: Recursively try all possibilities for '*'. O(3^n).
content.optimizedApproach: Greedy with range [lo, hi] tracking min/max possible open parentheses. '*' expands range; ')' shrinks it. Clamp lo to 0. Valid if lo == 0 at end.
content.keyInsight: Track [lo, hi] = possible open count range. lo never goes negative (clamp at 0). If hi < 0 at any point, it's invalid. End valid iff lo == 0.
content.pseudocode:
lo = hi = 0
for c in s:
    if c=='(': lo+=1; hi+=1
    elif c==')': lo-=1; hi-=1
    else: lo-=1; hi+=1
    if hi<0: return False
    lo = max(lo, 0)
return lo==0

content.problemStatement: n cars travel to the same destination at target miles. cars[i] starts at position[i] with speed[i]. Faster cars that catch a slower car merge into a fleet. Return the number of fleets.

content.problemStatement: Design a class StockSpanner where next(price) returns the span of the current day's stock price — the maximum number of consecutive days (starting from today and going backward) for which the stock price was less than or equal to today's price.

content.problemStatement: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar heights where the width of each bar is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.
content.naiveApproach: For each pair (i,j), find min height and compute area. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Monotonic stack (increasing). For each bar, pop shorter bars and compute the area they can support. A sentinel 0 at the end flushes remaining bars.
content.keyInsight: A bar can extend leftward as long as all bars to its left in the stack are taller. When a shorter bar arrives, compute the area the popped bar could form.
content.pseudocode:
stack=[(-1,-1)]; maxA=0
for i,h in enumerate(heights+[0]):
    while stack[-1][1]>h:
        idx, ht = stack.pop()
        w = i - stack[-1][0] - 1
        maxA = max(maxA, ht*w)
    stack.append((i,h))
return maxA

content.problemStatement: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index if found, otherwise -1.
content.optimizedApproach: Standard binary search: compare mid to target, halve the search space each iteration.
content.keyInsight: Each comparison eliminates half the remaining candidates. Invariant: target is always within [lo, hi].

l,r=0,len(nums)-1

    elif nums[m]<target: l=m+1
    else: r=m-1
return -1

content.problemStatement: A number 1..n is picked. Using API guess(num) which returns -1 (too high), 1 (too low), or 0 (correct), find the number.

l,r=1,n

content.problemStatement: Given a non-negative integer x, return the integer square root (floor).

l,r=0,x

return res

content.problemStatement: Given an m×n matrix where each row is sorted and the first element of each row is greater than the last of the previous row, search for a target integer.
content.optimizedApproach: Treat the matrix as a flattened sorted array. Binary search on indices 0..m*n-1, converting index to (row, col).

content.problemStatement: Koko has piles of bananas. She must eat all bananas within h hours, eating at most k bananas per hour from one pile. Find the minimum k.
content.naiveApproach: Try k=1,2,...,max(piles) and check feasibility. O(max_pile * n).
content.optimizedApproach: Binary search on k in [1..max(piles)]. For each candidate k, check if sum(ceil(pile/k)) <= h.
content.keyInsight: The feasibility function is monotonically decreasing in k. Binary search on the answer space — a standard pattern for minimization problems.

import math
l,r=1,max(piles)

while l<=r:
    k=(l+r)//2
    hours=sum(math.ceil(p/k) for p in piles)
    if hours<=h: res=k; r=k-1
    else: l=k+1
return res

content.problemTitle: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
content.problemStatement: Given weights and D days, find the minimum ship capacity so all packages are shipped in order within D days.

content.optimizedApproach: Binary search on capacity [max(weights)..sum(weights)]. Greedily fill each day to check feasibility.
content.keyInsight: Same binary-search-on-answer pattern as Koko. Minimum capacity is max(weights); maximum is sum(weights). Check: can we load all packages in D days?

l,r=max(weights),sum(weights)
while l<r:

    days=1;cur=0
    for w in weights:
        if cur+w>m: days+=1;cur=0
        cur+=w
    if days<=D: r=m
    else: l=m+1
return l

content.problemStatement: Given a sorted array arr, integer k, and integer x, return the k closest elements to x. Result should be sorted ascending.
content.naiveApproach: Binary search for x, expand outward with two pointers. O(log n + k).
content.optimizedApproach: Binary search for the left boundary of the window. Window arr[left..left+k-1] is valid if |arr[left]-x| <= |arr[left+k]-x|.
content.keyInsight: Binary search for the optimal window start: check if the left element or right element should be excluded by comparing distances to x.
content.pseudocode:
l,r=0,len(arr)-k
while l<r:
    m=(l+r)//2
    if x-arr[m]>arr[m+k]-x: l=m+1
    else: r=m
return arr[l:l+k]

content.problemStatement: Given a rotated sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return its index or -1.

content.keyInsight: At least one half is always sorted. If nums[l]<=nums[m], left half is sorted. Check if target is in the sorted half; if not, search the other.

l,r=0,len(nums)-1
while l<=r:

    if nums[l]<=nums[m]:
        if nums[l]<=target<nums[m]: r=m-1
        else: l=m+1
    else:
        if nums[m]<target<=nums[r]: l=m+1

return -1

content.problemStatement: Given array nums and integer k, split nums into k non-empty subarrays to minimize the largest subarray sum.
content.naiveApproach: DP: dp[i][j] = min largest sum for first i elements split into j parts. O(n²k).

content.keyInsight: Same binary-search-on-answer pattern. The check function greedily fills subarrays — greedy check is O(n), binary search is O(log sum).

l,r=max(nums),sum(nums)

content.problemStatement: Design a data structure that supports adding a number and finding the median. addNum(int num), findMedian() -> double.

content.problemStatement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the reversed list's head.
content.naiveApproach: Copy values to array, reverse, rebuild. O(n) but uses extra space.
content.optimizedApproach: Iterative with prev/cur pointers. Or recursive: reverse(head.next) then fix next pointer.
content.keyInsight: Three pointers: prev=None, cur=head. At each step: save next, point cur.next to prev, advance both. The trick is saving next before overwriting.
content.pseudocode:
prev,cur=None,head
while cur:
    nxt=cur.next
    cur.next=prev
    prev=cur
    cur=nxt
return prev

content.problemStatement: Merge two sorted linked lists and return as one sorted list.
content.constraints:
0<=n,m<=50
-100<=Node.val<=100
Both lists sorted in non-decreasing order
content.naiveApproach: Copy all nodes to array, sort, rebuild. O((n+m) log(n+m)).
content.optimizedApproach: Dummy head + two pointers: at each step take the smaller head, advance that pointer.
content.keyInsight: Dummy head simplifies edge cases (empty lists). Two pointers advance through each list; append remaining tail of the non-exhausted list.
content.pseudocode:
dummy=ListNode(0)
cur=dummy
while l1 and l2:
    if l1.val<=l2.val: cur.next=l1; l1=l1.next
    else: cur.next=l2; l2=l2.next
    cur=cur.next
cur.next=l1 or l2
return dummy.next

content.problemStatement: Given the head of a linked list, return true if the list has a cycle in it.
content.naiveApproach: Store visited nodes in a set. Return true if seen again. O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Floyd's cycle detection: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. If they meet, cycle exists.
content.keyInsight: Floyd's tortoise and hare: if a cycle exists, fast will lap slow. They will always meet within the cycle.
content.pseudocode:
slow=fast=head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow=slow.next
    fast=fast.next.next
    if slow==fast: return True
return False

content.problemStatement: Given the head of a linked list and integers left and right, reverse the nodes of the list from position left to right in one pass.
content.naiveApproach: Collect nodes in array, reverse subarray, rebuild links.
content.optimizedApproach: One pass: find the node before 'left', reverse the sublist in-place using prev/cur, reconnect.
content.keyInsight: Use a dummy head to handle left=1. Find the node just before position left. Then reverse right-left+1 nodes in-place, reconnecting both ends.
content.pseudocode:
dummy=ListNode(0,head);prev=dummy
for _ in range(left-1): prev=prev.next
cur=prev.next
for _ in range(right-left):
    nxt=cur.next
    cur.next=nxt.next
    nxt.next=prev.next
    prev.next=nxt
return dummy.next

content.problemTitle: Remove Nth Node From End of List
content.problemStatement: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return the head.
content.naiveApproach: Two passes: count length, then walk to (length-n)th node.
content.optimizedApproach: One pass: two pointers separated by n steps. When fast reaches end, slow is at the node to remove.
content.keyInsight: Maintain n+1 gap between fast and slow pointers. When fast hits null, slow.next is the target node. Dummy head handles removal of the first node.

dummy=ListNode(0,head)
fast=slow=dummy
for _ in range(n+1): fast=fast.next
while fast:
    fast=fast.next; slow=slow.next
slow.next=slow.next.next
return dummy.next

content.problemStatement: A linked list where each node has next and random pointers. Return a deep copy of the list.

random is null or points to a node in the list
content.naiveApproach: Two passes with a hash map: first pass creates copies, second assigns next/random.

content.problemStatement: Given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers stored in reverse order, add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.
content.naiveApproach: Convert to integers, add, convert back. May overflow for very large numbers.
content.optimizedApproach: Simulate addition with carry: step through both lists simultaneously, add digits plus carry, create new node.
content.keyInsight: Process digit by digit with a carry variable. Continue until both lists and carry are exhausted.
content.pseudocode:
dummy=ListNode(0);cur=dummy;carry=0
while l1 or l2 or carry:
    v1=l1.val if l1 else 0
    v2=l2.val if l2 else 0
    total=v1+v2+carry
    carry=total//10
    cur.next=ListNode(total%10)
    cur=cur.next
    if l1: l1=l1.next
    if l2: l2=l2.next
return dummy.next

content.problemStatement: Given array of n+1 integers where each is in [1,n], find the one duplicate number. Must not modify array, use O(1) extra space, O(n) time.
content.naiveApproach: HashSet to track seen numbers. O(n) space — violates constraint.
content.optimizedApproach: Floyd's cycle detection treating array values as pointers. The duplicate is the cycle entry point.
content.keyInsight: Index i points to nums[i], forming a functional graph. The duplicate creates two 'arrows' pointing to the same node — this is a cycle. Floyd's finds the entrance.
content.pseudocode:
slow=fast=nums[0]
while True:
    slow=nums[slow]
    fast=nums[nums[fast]]
    if slow==fast: break
slow2=nums[0]
while slow!=slow2:

content.problemStatement: Given head of a linked list L0→L1→…→Ln, reorder it to L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→L2→… in-place.
content.naiveApproach: Copy nodes to array, rebuild in required order. O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Three steps: (1) find middle (slow/fast), (2) reverse second half, (3) merge two halves alternately.
content.keyInsight: Split at middle, reverse the second half, then interleave. Each step uses well-known linked list techniques.
content.pseudocode:
# 1. Find middle
slow=fast=head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow=slow.next; fast=fast.next.next
# 2. Reverse second half
second=slow.next; slow.next=None
prev=None
while second:
    tmp=second.next; second.next=prev
    prev=second; second=tmp
# 3. Merge
first=head; second=prev
while second:
    tmp1=first.next; tmp2=second.next
    first.next=second; second.next=tmp1
    first=tmp1; second=tmp2

content.problemStatement: Design a Least Recently Used cache with get(key) and put(key,value) in O(1) time.
content.optimizedApproach: Doubly-linked list + hash map. List maintains order (MRU at head, LRU at tail). Dict maps key → node. O(1) remove-and-insert.
content.keyInsight: Hash map gives O(1) node lookup; doubly-linked list gives O(1) removal and insertion. Combine them: move accessed node to head, evict from tail.
content.pseudocode:
Use dummy head and tail nodes.
For get: look up node, move to head, return val.
For put: if exists, update and move to head.
  If new: create node, add to head.
  If over capacity: remove tail node and its dict entry.
followUpQuestions: Design a cache with O(1) all operations?

content.problemStatement: Design a circular queue (ring buffer) with enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, isFull operations.
content.naiveApproach: Dynamic list with mod index arithmetic.
content.optimizedApproach: Fixed-size array with head, tail, size counters. Modular arithmetic for circular indexing.
content.keyInsight: Use indices head and (head+size)%capacity for tail. Avoid size-1 ambiguity by tracking count separately.
content.pseudocode:
self.q=[0]*k; self.head=0; self.size=0; self.k=k
def enQueue(v): self.q[(self.head+self.size)%self.k]=v; self.size+=1
def deQueue(): self.head=(self.head+1)%self.k; self.size-=1

content.problemStatement: Design a Least Frequently Used cache. Ties broken by LRU. get(key) and put(key,value) in O(1).
content.naiveApproach: LRU cache + frequency counters. O(log n) with sorted structures.
content.optimizedApproach: Three maps: key→(val,freq), freq→OrderedDict(key→val), minFreq counter. On access, move key from freq[f] to freq[f+1].
content.keyInsight: Track minFreq globally. When frequency changes, update the freq→keys map. Use OrderedDict per frequency for LRU tiebreak within the same frequency.

from collections import defaultdict, OrderedDict
key_map={};freq_map=defaultdict(OrderedDict);min_freq=0
# get: update freq, return val
# put: if new and over capacity, evict freq_map[min_freq].popitem(last=False)

content.problemStatement: Merge k sorted linked lists and return it as one sorted list.
content.naiveApproach: Merge pairs one at a time k-1 times. O(kN) total where N is total nodes.
content.optimizedApproach: Min-heap of size k: push all heads, pop minimum and push its next repeatedly.
content.keyInsight: A min-heap keeps the current minimum across all k lists. Heap size stays k, giving O(log k) per extraction. Alternatively use divide & conquer merging.

content.problemStatement: Given the head of a linked list, reverse every k nodes. If remaining nodes < k, leave them as-is.
content.naiveApproach: Collect nodes in array, reverse in groups, rebuild. O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Find kth node, reverse group in-place, recurse/iterate for next group.
content.keyInsight: Before reversing, verify k nodes remain (getKth helper). After reversing a group, the original head becomes the tail — connect it to the result of the next group.
content.pseudocode:
def getKth(cur, k):
    while cur and k>0: cur=cur.next; k-=1
    return cur
dummy=ListNode(0,head); groupPrev=dummy
while True:
    kth=getKth(groupPrev,k)
    if not kth: break
    groupNext=kth.next
    # reverse [groupPrev.next .. kth]
    prev=groupNext; cur=groupPrev.next
    while cur!=groupNext:
        tmp=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=tmp
    tmp=groupPrev.next; groupPrev.next=kth; groupPrev=tmp
return dummy.next

content.problemTitle: Insert Greatest Common Divisors in Linked List
content.problemStatement: Given a linked list, insert a new node between every pair of adjacent nodes. The new node's value is the GCD of the two adjacent nodes' values.
content.naiveApproach: Traverse list, create new nodes with GCD, insert them — this is already optimal.
content.optimizedApproach: Same approach — traverse, compute gcd(a,b), insert new node between each pair.
content.keyInsight: Simple linked list traversal with insertion. GCD computation is O(log min(a,b)) per pair using Euclidean algorithm.
content.pseudocode:
from math import gcd
cur=head
while cur.next:
    val=gcd(cur.val,cur.next.val)
    new_node=ListNode(val,cur.next)
    cur.next=new_node
    cur=new_node.next
return head

content.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree and return its root. Swapping left and right children at every node.
content.naiveApproach: DFS iterative with stack. Same complexity.
content.optimizedApproach: Recursive: swap left/right, then recursively invert both subtrees.
content.keyInsight: Post-order or pre-order both work. Swap children first, then recurse on swapped children (or recurse then swap — equivalent).
content.pseudocode:
def invert(root):
    if not root: return None
    root.left,root.right=invert(root.right),invert(root.left)
    return root

content.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth (number of nodes along the longest root-to-leaf path).
content.optimizedApproach: Recursive DFS: depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
content.keyInsight: Tree depth = 1 + max subtree depths. Base case: None returns 0. Elegant one-liner with recursion.

content.problemStatement: Given a binary tree, return the length of the diameter (longest path between any two nodes, which may or may not pass through the root).
content.naiveApproach: At each node compute left depth + right depth; take max. O(n²) if depth is recomputed naively.
content.optimizedApproach: DFS that returns height while updating a global max diameter = left_height + right_height.
content.keyInsight: Diameter through a node = left_height + right_height. DFS returns height (max depth) bottom-up, updating the global diameter at each node.
content.pseudocode:
res=[0]
def dfs(node):
    if not node: return 0
    l=dfs(node.left); r=dfs(node.right)
    res[0]=max(res[0],l+r)
    return 1+max(l,r)
dfs(root); return res[0]

content.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced (every node's left and right subtrees differ in height by at most 1).
content.naiveApproach: At each node compute heights of both subtrees. O(n log n) with separate height calls.
content.optimizedApproach: DFS returning -1 for unbalanced or actual height. Short-circuits on first unbalanced subtree.
content.keyInsight: Return -1 as a sentinel for 'unbalanced'. If either child returns -1 or |left-right|>1, propagate -1 upward. This avoids recomputing heights.
content.pseudocode:
def height(node):
    if not node: return 0
    l=height(node.left)
    r=height(node.right)
    if l==-1 or r==-1 or abs(l-r)>1: return -1
    return 1+max(l,r)
return height(root)!=-1

content.problemStatement: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, return true if they are structurally identical and have the same node values.
content.naiveApproach: Serialize both trees and compare strings.
content.optimizedApproach: Recursive DFS: both null → true; one null or values differ → false; recurse on both sides.
content.keyInsight: Four cases: (null,null)→true, (null,x) or (x,null)→false, values differ→false, recurse both.

content.problemStatement: Given the roots of two binary trees root and subRoot, return true if there is a subtree of root with the same structure and node values as subRoot.
content.naiveApproach: For every node in root, check if it matches subRoot using isSameTree. O(m*n).
content.optimizedApproach: Same O(m*n) but with early termination via isSameTree. Or serialize both trees and do substring search O(m+n).
content.keyInsight: At every node, check isSameTree(node, subRoot). Recursively check both subtrees of root as well.
followUpQuestions: Serialize and use KMP for O(m+n) matching?

content.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, return the inorder traversal (left, root, right) of its node values.
content.naiveApproach: Recursive: recurse left, append, recurse right.
content.optimizedApproach: Iterative with explicit stack: push left spine, pop+visit, push right subtree.
content.keyInsight: Morris traversal achieves O(1) space using threading. For interviews, iterative with a stack is standard.
content.pseudocode:
res=[]; stack=[]; cur=root
while cur or stack:
    while cur: stack.append(cur); cur=cur.left
    cur=stack.pop(); res.append(cur.val); cur=cur.right
return res

content.problemStatement: Return the preorder traversal (root, left, right) of a binary tree's node values.
content.optimizedApproach: Iterative: push root, pop and visit, push right then left (so left is processed first).
content.keyInsight: For iterative preorder: push right before left so left is processed next (LIFO stack).
content.pseudocode:
stack=[root]; res=[]
while stack:
    node=stack.pop()
    if not node: continue
    res.append(node.val)
    stack.append(node.right)
    stack.append(node.left)
return res

content.problemStatement: Return the postorder traversal (left, right, root) of a binary tree's node values.
content.optimizedApproach: Iterative: modified preorder (root, right, left) then reverse the result gives (left, right, root).
content.keyInsight: Reverse of (root→right→left) preorder = postorder. Or use two stacks.
content.pseudocode:
stack=[root]; res=[]
while stack:
    node=stack.pop()
    if not node: continue
    res.append(node.val)
    stack.append(node.left)
    stack.append(node.right)
return res[::-1]

content.problemStatement: Return the level order traversal of a binary tree's values (BFS, level by level).
content.optimizedApproach: BFS with a queue. For each level, process all nodes and enqueue their children.
content.keyInsight: Process level by level: queue size at the start of each iteration equals nodes at that level. Snapshot the size before the inner loop.

content.problemStatement: Given a binary tree, return the values of nodes visible from the right side when viewed top-to-bottom.
content.naiveApproach: BFS level order, take last element of each level.
content.optimizedApproach: BFS (same as level order) taking last node per level. Or DFS visiting right before left, recording first node at each new depth.
content.keyInsight: The rightmost visible node per level is the last node in BFS. DFS right-first also works: record val if depth == len(res).

content.problemTitle: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
content.problemStatement: Given a binary tree, a node X is good if in the path from root to X there are no nodes with a value greater than X's value. Return the number of good nodes.
content.naiveApproach: Track path values to each node. O(n*h) naively.
content.optimizedApproach: DFS passing the maximum value seen on the path so far. Node is good if node.val >= max_so_far.
content.keyInsight: A node is 'good' if it's the maximum on its root-to-node path. Pass max_so_far top-down; no backtracking needed.

content.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid BST.
content.naiveApproach: In-order traversal and check if sorted. O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: DFS with min/max bounds. At each node, check min < node.val < max; pass updated bounds to children.
content.keyInsight: BST constraint is global: all nodes in left subtree < current < all nodes in right subtree. Passing (min, max) bounds propagates this constraint down.

content.problemTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
content.problemStatement: Given a BST, find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes p and q.
content.constraints:
2<=n<=10^5
-10^9<=Node.val<=10^9
p!=q, both exist in the tree
content.naiveApproach: DFS/BFS to find paths from root to both nodes, then find LCA. O(n).
content.optimizedApproach: Exploit BST property: if both p,q < root, go left; if both > root, go right; else root is LCA.
content.keyInsight: In a BST, the LCA is the first node where p and q split directions. If both are on the same side, move that direction.
content.pseudocode:
cur=root
while cur:
    if p.val<cur.val and q.val<cur.val: cur=cur.left
    elif p.val>cur.val and q.val>cur.val: cur=cur.right
    else: return cur

content.problemTitle: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
content.problemStatement: Given the root of a BST and an integer k, return the kth smallest value.
content.naiveApproach: Collect all values with inorder traversal, return index k-1. O(n) space.
content.optimizedApproach: Iterative inorder traversal (Morris or stack): stop and return at the kth node visited.
content.keyInsight: Inorder traversal of BST yields sorted order. The kth node visited in inorder is the kth smallest.
content.pseudocode:
stack=[]; cur=root; k=k
while stack or cur:
    while cur: stack.append(cur); cur=cur.left
    cur=stack.pop(); k-=1
    if k==0: return cur.val
    cur=cur.right

content.problemTitle: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
content.problemStatement: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder, construct and return the binary tree.
content.naiveApproach: Scan inorder linearly to find root index each time. O(n²).
content.optimizedApproach: Hash map of inorder values to indices for O(1) root lookup. Recursively build with pointer arithmetic.
content.keyInsight: preorder[0] is always the root. Its index in inorder divides into left (elements before) and right (elements after) subtrees. preorder left subtree starts at index 1 for size = left_size.
content.pseudocode:
idx_map={v:i for i,v in enumerate(inorder)}
pre_idx=0
def build(l,r):
    nonlocal pre_idx
    if l>r: return None
    root_val=preorder[pre_idx]; pre_idx+=1
    root=TreeNode(root_val)
    mid=idx_map[root_val]
    root.left=build(l,mid-1)
    root.right=build(mid+1,r)
    return root
return build(0,len(inorder)-1)

content.problemStatement: Given a root of a BST and a key, delete the node with that key and return the updated root.
content.constraints:
0<=n<=10^4
-10^5<=Node.val<=10^5
Each node has a unique value
content.naiveApproach: Find node, handle three cases manually. O(h).
content.optimizedApproach: Recursive: if key < root → recurse left; if key > root → recurse right; if found → replace with inorder successor (min of right subtree) or predecessor.
content.keyInsight: Three cases when found: (1) no children → return null; (2) one child → return that child; (3) two children → find inorder successor (min in right subtree), copy its value, delete successor.

content.problemTitle: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
content.problemStatement: Given the root of a BST and a value val, insert val into the BST and return the root.
content.naiveApproach: Traverse to the correct insertion point iteratively.
content.optimizedApproach: Recursive: if val < root.val, recurse left; if val > root.val, recurse right; if null, return new node.
content.keyInsight: BST property tells you exactly which direction to go. Insertion is always at a leaf position.

content.problemStatement: The thief has found a house in a tree. Adjacent connected houses cannot be robbed on the same night. Return the maximum amount of money possible.
content.naiveApproach: For each subtree, try robbing root or not. Exponential without memoization.
content.optimizedApproach: DFS returning pair (rob, skip): rob=node.val + skip_left + skip_right; skip=max(rob,skip)_left + max(rob,skip)_right.
content.keyInsight: Each node returns two values: max if we rob this node, and max if we skip it. The parent decides based on these pairs without re-computing.

content.problemTitle: Delete Leaves With a Given Value
content.problemStatement: Given a binary tree and an integer target, delete all leaf nodes with value equal to target. Repeat until no more such leaves exist.
content.naiveApproach: Multiple passes until no change. O(n * passes).
content.optimizedApproach: Post-order DFS: recursively remove leaves in subtrees first, then check if current node is now a leaf with target value.
content.keyInsight: Post-order (bottom-up) handles cascading deletion naturally: after children are pruned, the current node may become a leaf worth deleting.
content.pseudocode:
def removeLeafNodes(root,target):
    if not root: return None
    root.left=removeLeafNodes(root.left,target)
    root.right=removeLeafNodes(root.right,target)
    if not root.left and not root.right and root.val==target:
        return None
    return root

content.problemStatement: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes has an edge. The path sum is the sum of the node values. Return the maximum path sum (path can start/end at any node).
content.optimizedApproach: DFS returning max gain from each node to its subtree. At each node, update global max with left_gain + node.val + right_gain. Return node.val + max(left,right,0).
content.keyInsight: A path through a node contributes: max(0,left_gain) + node.val + max(0,right_gain). But the return value for parent contribution is node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain, 0) (path can only go one direction up).
content.pseudocode:
res=[float('-inf')]
def dfs(node):
    if not node: return 0
    l=max(dfs(node.left),0)
    r=max(dfs(node.right),0)
    res[0]=max(res[0],node.val+l+r)
    return node.val+max(l,r)
dfs(root); return res[0]

content.problemStatement: Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree. The encoding/decoding scheme is your choice.
content.optimizedApproach: Pre-order DFS with null markers ('null'). Serialize: root,left,right. Deserialize: use a queue of tokens, pop front to build each node.
content.keyInsight: Pre-order with explicit nulls uniquely encodes a binary tree. Deserialization consumes tokens in the same pre-order — one token per recursive call.

content.constraints:
1<=word.length<=2000
word consists of lowercase English letters
At most 3*10^4 calls
content.naiveApproach: Hash set for full words. Doesn't support prefix search efficiently.
content.optimizedApproach: Trie with TrieNode (array of 26 children + is_end flag). Each operation traverses the trie character by character.

optimizedComplexity.time: O(m) per op where m=word length

content.keyInsight: Each TrieNode stores 26 children (one per letter) and an is_end flag. Insert creates nodes as needed; search returns false if any node is missing.

content.problemTitle: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
content.problemStatement: Design a data structure that supports addWord and search. search(word) can match any word with '.' where '.' can represent any letter.
content.constraints:
1<=word.length<=25
word consists of lowercase letters or '.'
At most 10^4 calls

content.optimizedApproach: Trie with recursive DFS for '.' wildcard: try all 26 children at wildcard positions.

content.problemStatement: Given an m×n board of characters and a list of strings words, return all words on the board. Each letter may only be used once per path.
content.naiveApproach: Run Word Search I for each word. O(words * m * n * 4^len).
content.optimizedApproach: Build a Trie from all words. Single DFS over the board — at each cell traverse the Trie simultaneously. Prune branches not in Trie.

content.problemTitle: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
content.problemStatement: Design a class that finds the kth largest element in a stream. add(val) adds element and returns kth largest.
content.optimizedApproach: Min-heap of size k. Root = kth largest.
content.keyInsight: Min-heap of size k keeps the k largest. Root is the kth largest.

content.problemStatement: Smash two heaviest stones; if equal both destroyed, else larger becomes y-x. Return weight of last stone or 0.
content.optimizedApproach: Max-heap. Pop two maxima, push y-x if nonzero.
content.keyInsight: Max-heap via negation (Python min-heap).

import heapq
stones=[-s for s in stones]
heapq.heapify(stones)
while len(stones)>1:
    y=-heapq.heappop(stones); x=-heapq.heappop(stones)
    if y!=x: heapq.heappush(stones,-(y-x))

content.problemStatement: Find k closest points to origin. Order does not matter.
content.optimizedApproach: Max-heap of size k. Push each point; pop if size > k.
content.keyInsight: Max-heap keeps k smallest distances. Compare squared distances.

content.problemTitle: Kth Largest Element in an Array
content.problemStatement: Return the kth largest element (not kth distinct).
content.optimizedApproach: Min-heap size k O(n log k) or QuickSelect O(n) average.
content.keyInsight: Min-heap root = kth largest. QuickSelect partitions around pivot recursively.

content.problemStatement: CPU tasks A-Z with cooldown n. Return minimum intervals to finish all tasks.
content.optimizedApproach: Max-heap + cooldown queue. Or math formula.
content.keyInsight: Most frequent task defines frame. Fill gaps with other tasks, else idle.

content.problemStatement: postTweet, getNewsFeed (10 most recent tweets), follow, unfollow.
content.naiveApproach: Store all tweets; merge on getFeed.
content.optimizedApproach: user→tweets (timestamped) and user→followees maps. Merge heads with max-heap.
content.keyInsight: Merge K sorted lists pattern with heap.

content.problemStatement: Rearrange so no two adjacent chars are same. Return result or '' if impossible.
content.optimizedApproach: Max-heap by frequency. Alternate most frequent.
content.keyInsight: Max freq > (n+1)//2 → impossible. Greedy: alternate most frequent.
content.pseudocode:
from collections import Counter; import heapq
count=Counter(s)
heap=[(-c,char) for char,c in count.items()]
heapq.heapify(heap); prev=(0,''); res=[]
while heap:
    c,char=heapq.heappop(heap)
    res.append(char)
    if prev[0]<0: heapq.heappush(heap,prev)
    prev=(c+1,char)
return ''.join(res) if len(res)==len(s) else ''

content.problemStatement: k projects with profit[i] and capital[i], start with w capital. Maximize capital after at most k projects.
content.naiveApproach: Scan all affordable projects each round.
content.optimizedApproach: Sort by capital. Max-heap for profits of affordable projects.
content.keyInsight: Greedy: always pick max profit among affordable. Add newly affordable as w grows.
content.pseudocode:
projects=sorted(zip(capital,profits)); max_heap=[]; i=0
for _ in range(k):
    while i<len(projects) and projects[i][0]<=w:
        heapq.heappush(max_heap,-projects[i][1]); i+=1
    if not max_heap: break
    w-=heapq.heappop(max_heap)
return w

content.problemStatement: FreqStack push(val) and pop() returning most frequently pushed (ties: most recent).
content.naiveApproach: Scan for max frequency on pop.
content.optimizedApproach: val→freq map and freq→stack map. Track max_freq.
content.keyInsight: Map each frequency level to a stack. Pop max_freq stack; decrement max_freq if empty.
content.pseudocode:
self.freq=defaultdict(int); self.group=defaultdict(list); self.max_freq=0
def push(val):
    self.freq[val]+=1; f=self.freq[val]
    self.max_freq=max(self.max_freq,f); self.group[f].append(val)
def pop():
    val=self.group[self.max_freq].pop(); self.freq[val]-=1
    if not self.group[self.max_freq]: self.max_freq-=1
    return val

content.problemStatement: Tasks [enqueueTime,processingTime]. Pick smallest processing time when free. Return processing order.
content.optimizedApproach: Sort by enqueue time. Min-heap for available tasks. Jump time when idle.
content.keyInsight: When idle jump to next enqueue time. Add all available tasks to heap.
content.pseudocode:
tasks=sorted(enumerate(tasks),key=lambda x:x[1][0])
heap=[]; time=0; i=0; res=[]
while len(res)<len(tasks):
    while i<len(tasks) and tasks[i][1][0]<=time:
        heapq.heappush(heap,(tasks[i][1][1],tasks[i][0])); i+=1
    if not heap: time=tasks[i][1][0]; continue
    pt,idx=heapq.heappop(heap); time+=pt; res.append(idx)
return res

content.problemStatement: Given unique integers, return all possible subsets (power set).
content.optimizedApproach: Backtracking: at each index include or exclude.
content.keyInsight: 2^n subsets. Add current subset at each call, recurse with next index.

content.problemStatement: Given distinct candidates, return all unique combinations summing to target. Same number may be used unlimited times.
content.optimizedApproach: Backtracking: pass same index i to allow reuse; i+1 prevents.
content.keyInsight: Pass same i (not i+1) to allow reuse. Sort to enable pruning.
content.pseudocode:
res=[]
def backtrack(idx,comb,remain):
    if remain==0: res.append(comb[:]); return
    for i in range(idx,len(candidates)):
